extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of science; readers interested in philosophy/methods of science
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for judging when conceptions, observations, and inferences qualify as scientifically valid — covering criteria like self-consistency, deducibility from normal perception, repeatability, logical drawability, and limits of legitimate inference (e.g., about consciousness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure of consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: The measure of consciousness will thus largely depend on (i) the extent and variety of past sense-impressions, and (2) the degree to which the brain can permanently preserve the impress of these sense-impressions, or what might be termed the complexity and plasticity of the brain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consciousness is tied to stored sensory history and the brain's capacity to retain and combine impressions. Use these two dimensions (variety/extent of impressions; permanence/plasticity of storage) when assessing degree of consciousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary versus involuntary action
rubrics_metrics.description: When an exertion follows immediately on a sense-impression we speak of the exertion as involuntary ... On the other hand, when the exertion is conditioned by stored sense-impresses we term our action voluntary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish actions determined solely by immediate sensory input (involuntary / mechanically controlled) from those conditioned by stored impressions or past training (voluntary, attributable to 'within'). The telephone-exchange analogy illustrates habitual/mechanical linking versus considered linking based on stored information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought as sparked by immediate sense-impressions interacting with stored impressions
rubrics_metrics.description: The immediate sense-impression is to be looked upon as the spark which kindles thought, which brings into play the still remaining impresses of past sense-impressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating accounts of thought, require an account of how immediate impressions interact with stored impressions; be cautious that causal chains may be complex and not always traceable, but accept that elements of thought are ultimately derived from past impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific validity of a conception
rubrics_metrics.description: In order that a conception may have scientific validity, it must be self-consistent, and deducible from the perceptions of the normal human being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check (a) internal self-consistency (not self-negating, e.g., centaur), and (b) deducibility from the perceptions of a normal human observer. Account for atypical perceptual faculties (e.g., colour-blindness) — such conceptions may be studied scientifically as abnormalities but lack general scientific validity. Also consider whether properly trained observers in suitable circumstances would derive the conception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of repeatability and multiple observers
rubrics_metrics.description: The observations and experiments of science should be repeated as often and by as many observers as possible, in order to ensure that we are dealing with what has validity for all normal human beings, and not with the results of an abnormal perceptive faculty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize replication and independent observation. For unique or non-repeatable events place a high burden on recorders and the wider community to test observer normality, training, emotional state, and conditions; prefer scepticism and critical probing over credulity. (Example: Brown-Sequard's contentious hereditary disease experiments.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific validity of an inference
rubrics_metrics.description: The inference which is scientifically valid is that which could be drawn by every logically trained normal mind, if it were in possession of the conceptions upon which the inference has been based.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish 'could be drawn' from 'would be drawn' — logical validity is about what trained minds ought to infer given the premises. Account for social/institutional inertia and bias that delay acceptance (e.g., Darwin). Insist on logical training and clear premises for inferences to be counted scientific.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject argument-from-ignorance as proof
rubrics_metrics.description: The assumption ... that the strongest argument in favour of the truth of a statement is the absence or impossibility of a demonstration of its falsehood is fallacious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat absence of disproof as weak evidence; beware inferences that substitute impossibility of disproof for positive supporting evidence. Examples provided include supernatural/materialization claims, appeals to science to confirm metaphysical hopes, and sweeping claims about consciousness of matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on inferring other-consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Where no like machinery, no like interval can be observed, there we have no right to infer any consciousness. ... From will and consciousness associated with material machinery we can infer nothing whatever as to will and consciousness without that machinery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infer consciousness in other beings only when analogous physiological machinery and the temporal interval between sensation and action (indicative of internal processing) are observable. Do not extend inference to entities lacking nervous systems or to purely immaterial postulates without material correlates; such extrapolations exceed scientific inference and may be self-contradictory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science operates on conceptions derived from sense-impressions
rubrics_metrics.description: The object of the present work is to insist ... that science is in reality a classification and analysis of the contents of the mind; and the scientific method consists in drawing just comparisons and inferences from the stored impresses of past sense-impressions ... Not till the immediate sense-impression has reached the level of a conception, or at least a perception, does it become material for science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging scientific claims, expect that raw sensory input has been processed into concepts, classifications, and abstractions before scientific treatment. Recognize that many scientific hypotheses lie beyond immediate sensation and are legitimate when properly derived from and connected back to sensory data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canon of belief: apply reason before belief
rubrics_metrics.description: Where it is impossible to apply man's reason, that is to criticise and investigate at all, there it is not only unprofitable but anti-social to believe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat belief as an adjunct to knowledge used to guide action under weighed probability; avoid holding beliefs in domains where critical inquiry and reasoning are impossible, because such beliefs can prejudice reasoning in other domains. Encourage shifting from uncritical faith to probability-weighted conviction via critique.
